title: What can you say about turmeric (curcumin) in your ads and on your site?
summary: The library supports 3 wordings for turmeric (curcumin); the strongest is "Used in herbal medicine to aid digestion" (moderate, 1-9 g dried rhizome (or crude equivalent) a day). Avoid wording that names or implies a disease, a drug or a treatment, such as "Relieves joint pain, arthritis or inflammation".

supported_wordings.wording: A source of antioxidants that help protect cells against damage from free radicals.
supported_wordings.why: Health Canada sets maximum doses only, with no minimum; no other listed source covers it.
supported_wordings.daily_dose: up to 9 g dried rhizome (or crude equivalent) a day
supported_wordings.dose_details: Adults 18 and older. Concentrated extracts: up to 1,500 mg curcuminoids a day and 500 mg per dose; curcumin: up to 1,200 mg a day and 400 mg per dose.
supported_wordings.form: Turmeric rhizome or extracts; curcuminoids; curcumin

sources.name: Health Canada monograph: Concentrated turmeric and isolates (curcuminoids/curcumin)

supported_wordings.wording: Used in herbal medicine to aid digestion.
supported_wordings.why: Health Canada lists it as a herbal medicine use at 1-9 g a day; no other listed source covers it.
supported_wordings.daily_dose: 1-9 g dried rhizome (or crude equivalent) a day

supported_wordings.wording: Traditionally used in herbal medicine to help relieve occasional indigestion with gas.
supported_wordings.why: Traditional use in Health Canada's monograph; no other listed source covers it.
supported_wordings.daily_dose: 1-9 g dried rhizome (or crude equivalent) a day
supported_wordings.dose_details: Adults 18 and older. The 'occasional' form keeps the wording in structure-and-function territory.

wordings_to_avoid.wording: Relieves joint pain, arthritis or inflammation
wordings_to_avoid.why: FDA's 2000 rule (page 1016) says 'joint pain' is characteristic of arthritis.

wordings_to_avoid.wording: A natural anti-inflammatory, or works like ibuprofen
wordings_to_avoid.why: Presents the product as a drug substitute.
Implies protection against liver disease; Health Canada also warns about liver problems with turmeric and curcumin.

evidence_strengths.strong: At least two listed sources support it independently at a comparable dose and form, and none disagrees.
evidence_strengths.moderate: One listed source supports it as an evidence-based use at that dose, and no listed source disagrees.
evidence_strengths.limited: The only support is traditional use, the sources disagree, or the source itself calls the evidence weak.

reasons_to_avoid.drug: names a drug or presents the product as one
reasons_to_avoid.treatment: promises to treat, cure or prevent a condition

sources.name: Health Canada monograph: Concentrated turmeric and isolates (curcuminoids/curcumin)
FDA final rule on structure/function statements, 65 FR 1000 (6 January 2000), page 1031

disclaimer: Not legal advice. This guide shows the wording that published evidence supports at a daily dose, from the sources linked below; it is not a ruling on any claim. Your own product, its form and dose, and your own evidence still need to match the wording you use.
